transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, it's... well, it's nice to meet you too, I suppose. I'm here because things have just gotten completely out of hand at work, and honestly, in my head, too. I'm an industrial production manager, and for the last few weeks, maybe months—time is a little blurry—I was just on fire. I mean, absolutely unstoppable. I was launching all these massive plant redesign projects, like, totally overhauling the assembly line flow because I suddenly saw exactly how to optimize the whole floor. I was staying up half the night, calling our overseas suppliers at, like, 2 AM my time because I just couldn't wait until morning to finalize the raw material shipments. I even completely rewrote the entire shift schedule for all three floors—by myself, in one weekend—because the old system was just too inefficient and I knew I could fix it. I felt like I could do the work of ten people, and I was, I really was. But then... it just stopped. Like hitting a brick wall. And now, I'm sitting here, and I can't even look at the spreadsheets I made. I can't keep up with the very projects I forced into motion. The emails are piling up, the suppliers are calling me back, and I just... I can't do it. I can't even get out of bed some mornings to face the mess I made when I was feeling so brilliant. It's like I built this massive, speeding train and then just forgot how to drive it, and now it's crashing. So, yeah, that's... that's why I'm here.
During that time when you felt unstoppable, did you have beliefs or experiences that other people said were not real?

No, no, it wasn't like that. I wasn't... making things up or seeing things that weren't there, if that's what you mean. Everything I was doing was completely based in reality. I mean, the plant redesign? That was based on actual throughput data from the last three quarters. I pulled the reports myself, line by line. My boss, David, he did say to me at one point, "You're living in a fantasy world if you think we can implement this by Q3," but he didn't mean I was literally hallucinating or out of touch with reality. He just meant the timeline was too aggressive for our current budget constraints and the union rules. 

And sure, the overseas suppliers thought I was a bit intense calling at 2 AM, and maybe my coworkers thought I was going overboard because I had blueprints spread all over the conference room table for a week straight, but the raw materials I was ordering were real. The supply chain bottlenecks I was fixing were real problems we've been having since last November. So, no, nobody was telling me I was seeing things or having fake experiences or anything bizarre like that. I was just... I was connecting dots that were actually there, just, you know, connecting them really, really fast. Too fast, obviously, since now I'm paying for it and the whole thing is a disaster. But it was all real. It was all real work, real spreadsheets, real data.
During that time when you felt unstoppable, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

Oh, absolutely. It was honestly bizarre, looking back on it now, but at the time, it felt like a superpower. Sleep just felt completely unnecessary. I mean, usually, I’m someone who needs a solid seven or eight hours, or I’m dragging the next day, right? But during those weeks, I’d be up until 3 or 4 in the morning, staring at my dual monitors, color-coding the shift schedules and cross-referencing the supplier logistics, and then I’d just lay down for maybe two or three hours. And the crazy thing is, my alarm would go off at 6 AM, and I wouldn’t even hit snooze. I’d just pop right up, wide awake. 

I was showing up at the plant before anyone else, feeling completely sharp and charged. I’d be walking the floor with my clipboard, already firing off instructions before the foremen even had their first cup of coffee. I remember thinking that sleep was just this... this optional thing, you know? Like it was a biological inefficiency that I had somehow evolved past. I’d even tell my husband, "Why waste a third of your life unconscious when there's so much to do?" I felt so energized, like my blood was carbonated. I didn't feel tired at all, not even a little bit. It was just go, go, go, all day, all night. And now, of course, all I want to do is sleep, which is the ultimate irony, isn't it? But back then... yeah, two or three hours was all I needed, and I felt like I could conquer the world on it.
During that period when you felt unstoppable, were you hospitalized because of it?

No, no, I wasn't hospitalized. Nothing like that. I mean, I was definitely running at a million miles an hour, and my husband was practically begging me to slow down—he kept saying I was going to burn myself out, which, you know, he was right about, obviously. He even threatened to call my sister to come stay with us because he didn't know what to do with me pacing the living room at 4 AM, talking about supply chain optimization. But no one ever mentioned a hospital. 

I think because I was still going to work every day, right? I was still putting on my suit, driving to the plant, and technically doing my job—just doing it way too intensely and making a huge mess of it. It wasn't like I was a danger to anyone or anything. I wasn't doing anything illegal or unsafe, just... overhauling assembly lines and sending a hundred emails a day. So, no, I never ended up in a hospital or an emergency room or anything like that. I just kept pushing until I completely crashed on my own couch, and that's where I've basically been ever since. But yeah, no hospital. Just a really, really hard landing back into reality.
During that time when you felt unstoppable, did your behavior cause serious problems at work or at home?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it’s embarrassing to even talk about now, considering how capable I usually am. I’m the person people come to when they need things fixed, you know? But during that time... I was just so scattered, so overwhelmed by all the brilliant ideas I thought I had, that I actually couldn't do my real job. 

There was this one day, specifically. We had this massive shift-planning meeting. It’s a quarterly thing, incredibly important for production forecasting, and I was supposed to lead it. I walked in there with my three binders full of the redesign plans I'd been working on all night, and I just... I couldn't focus on the actual agenda. They were asking me basic questions about headcount and overtime budgets for the next month, and I couldn't answer them. I couldn't even process what they were saying because my brain was ten steps ahead, thinking about reorganizing the entire floor layout. I started talking over people, jumping from topic to topic, and I could see them all just staring at me. David, my boss, was looking at me like I was an alien. 

I actually had to stop, right in the middle of a sentence, and just ask to be pulled out of the meeting. I just said, "I have to go," and I walked out. It was mortifying. And then, because of that, occupational health had to get involved. HR flagged it because I literally wasn’t able to carry out the basic production decisions my role depends on. They had me sit down with the company nurse, and she was asking me all these questions about my stress levels and if I was sleeping—which, you know, I wasn't, but I told her I was fine. But yeah, it caused huge problems. I had to take a few days of PTO just to let things cool down, and even now, David is double-checking all my reports, which he never used to do. It’s like I completely shattered my own professional reputation in a matter of weeks. And at home... well, my husband is barely talking to me right now because he's so exhausted from dealing with me. So, yes, serious problems. Everywhere.
Before this recent period, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt unusually energized or high like that?

No... no, never. Honestly, that’s what makes this whole thing so terrifying for me. I’ve always been the steady one, you know? I’m 29, I’ve been working in industrial production since I finished my master's, and I have always, always been the reliable, level-headed person that everyone counts on to not lose their cool when a supplier backs out at the last minute or a machine goes down. 

Even back in grad school, when everyone else in my cohort was pulling all-nighters and drinking those awful energy drinks and bouncing off the walls during finals week, I wasn't doing that. I was the one who had my study schedule mapped out weeks in advance so I could still get my eight hours of sleep. I've just never operated like that. So, no, I’ve never felt anything even close to this before. I’ve never had this... this bizarre surge of energy or felt like my brain was running on a completely different operating system. 

I mean, sure, I get excited about a good production yield or a successful safety audit, who doesn't? But that’s just normal professional satisfaction. It’s not this unstoppable, vibrating, carbonated feeling I had a few weeks ago. That was entirely new. And it’s just so wildly out of character for me, which is probably why David was so shocked in that meeting, and why my husband is struggling so much to understand what's happening right now. They’ve known me for years and they’ve never seen me like that, because I’ve never *been* like that. Not once. It really was just this one, massive... explosion, I guess you could call it. It came completely out of nowhere. So, yeah, nothing before this. Never.
Since the crash, have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yes. It’s... it’s all day. Every single day. I know I just said I crashed on my own couch, but actually, things got so incredibly strained at home with my husband that we decided I needed to give him some space. The tension was just suffocating. So I’m staying in this furnished temporary apartment right now, just a short-term lease a few miles away. 

And lately, I wake up in the temporary apartment with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the day is already ruined before I even drive to the plant. It’s there before I even open my eyes. Before the alarm even goes off, I can feel this crushing weight sitting right in the middle of my chest, and it just... it doesn't go away. You’d think that getting up, taking a shower, putting on my work clothes would help shake it off, but it doesn't. 

I drag myself out the door, and that hollow feeling just rides in the passenger seat with me all the way to work. And when I get to the production floor, where I’m usually so engaged and focused, I just feel entirely empty. I sit in my office looking at the exact same forecasting reports I was so obsessed with a month ago, and I feel absolutely nothing but this deep, dark slump. It’s not just a passing sadness or feeling a little down because I messed up at work. It’s constant. From the second I wake up in that quiet, strange apartment until the minute I finally manage to go back to sleep, it’s just this unending, heavy fog. I just can't seem to escape it for even an hour.
Since the crash, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living or that you might harm yourself?

No, no, I haven't. I mean, I know how it sounds, with everything I just said about the heavy fog and the crushing weight and waking up in that strange apartment feeling so hollow, but I haven't actually thought about... doing anything like that. It's more of a... a complete absence of joy or motivation, you know? Not a desire to end things. 

I think about my job, and even though I've damaged my reputation and David is hovering over me, I still care about the plant. I still care about the production lines running smoothly, even if I can't muster the energy to actually do the work right now. And my husband... even though we're separated at the moment and he's exhausted, I still want to fix things with him. I don't want to just give up. 

It's just that it's so hard to see how things get better when you're in the middle of it. When every single day feels like you're walking through wet concrete, it's hard to imagine ever feeling light again. But no, I haven't had any thoughts of harming myself. I've never been the type to think that way, even now, when things are arguably the worst they've ever been in my entire life. I just want this awful, heavy feeling to stop, but I don't want to... you know, I don't want to not be here. I just want to be myself again.
About how long did that period of feeling unstoppable last?

Well, the unstoppable part, that vibrating, carbonated feeling... that lasted for maybe a week, week and a half before everything just completely shattered. But this other part, this... this intense shift from being in total overdrive to barely being able to function at all? That's been going on since I moved into the temporary apartment. Which was about three weeks ago. 

It feels like a lifetime, honestly. Three weeks of just... waking up in a bed that isn't mine, staring at a ceiling fan that makes this weird clicking noise, and just feeling completely empty. It's so strange how quickly it flipped. One minute I was convinced I could optimize the entire global supply chain single-handedly, and the next, I'm sitting on a rented sofa from a corporate housing catalog, unable to even decide what to eat for dinner. It's been exactly three weeks of this heavy, suffocating fog, and it hasn't lifted for a single second. I keep looking at the calendar on my phone, trying to pinpoint exactly when the switch flipped, but it all just blurs together into this one long, exhausting slump since I packed that overnight bag and left the house. Three weeks. It feels like three years.

Yes. It’s... it’s all day. Every single day. I know I just said I crashed on my own couch, but actually, things got so incredibly strained at home with my husband that we decided I needed to give him some space. The tension was just suffocating. So I’m staying in this furnished temporary apartment right now, just a short-term lease a few miles away. 

And lately, I wake up in the temporary apartment with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the day is already ruined before I even drive to the plant. It’s there before I even open my eyes. Before the alarm even goes off, I can feel this crushing weight sitting right in the middle of my chest, and it just... it doesn't go away. You’d think that getting up, taking a shower, putting on my work clothes would help shake it off, but it doesn't. 

I drag myself out the door, and that hollow feeling just rides in the passenger seat with me all the way to work. And when I get to the production floor, where I’m usually so engaged and focused, I just feel entirely empty. I sit in my office looking at the exact same forecasting reports I was so obsessed with a month ago, and I feel absolutely nothing but this deep, dark slump. It’s not just a passing sadness or feeling a little down because I messed up at work. It’s constant. From the second I wake up in that quiet, strange apartment until the minute I finally manage to go back to sleep, it’s just this unending, heavy fog. I just can't seem to escape it for even an hour.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes suicidal ideation, which would support major depressive episode severity and guide diagnosis and risk assessment.
doctor.question: Since the crash, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living or that you might harm yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal thoughts or self-harm, which is not covered by any of the items in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, I haven't. I mean, I know how it sounds, with everything I just said about the heavy fog and the crushing weight and waking up in that strange apartment feeling so hollow, but I haven't actually thought about... doing anything like that. It's more of a... a complete absence of joy or motivation, you know? Not a desire to end things. 

I think about my job, and even though I've damaged my reputation and David is hovering over me, I still care about the plant. I still care about the production lines running smoothly, even if I can't muster the energy to actually do the work right now. And my husband... even though we're separated at the moment and he's exhausted, I still want to fix things with him. I don't want to just give up. 

It's just that it's so hard to see how things get better when you're in the middle of it. When every single day feels like you're walking through wet concrete, it's hard to imagine ever feeling light again. But no, I haven't had any thoughts of harming myself. I've never been the type to think that way, even now, when things are arguably the worst they've ever been in my entire life. I just want this awful, heavy feeling to stop, but I don't want to... you know, I don't want to not be here. I just want to be myself again.

inference.note: Current history supports a first manic episode without psychotic symptoms: markedly decreased need for sleep, elevated/expansive energy, increased goal-directed activity, functional impairment at work/home, and no psychosis or hospitalization. The current depressive symptoms occurring after mania make a unipolar depressive episode (F32.2) less likely and suggest bipolar affective disorder; because this appears to be a manic episode, F31.1 is favored, with F31.9 retained until full episode duration/exclusion details are confirmed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated episode lasted at least 1 week, which distinguishes a manic episode (bipolar I disorder, current/manic episode) from a shorter or unspecified bipolar presentation.
doctor.question: About how long did that period of feeling unstoppable last?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The intense shift from overdrive to barely functioning has been going on since I moved into the temporary apartment about three weeks ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the 'unstoppable' (hypomanic) period, which corresponds to the general duration key detailing the timeline of the recent episode.

patient.answer:
Well, the unstoppable part, that vibrating, carbonated feeling... that lasted for maybe a week, week and a half before everything just completely shattered. But this other part, this... this intense shift from being in total overdrive to barely being able to function at all? That's been going on since I moved into the temporary apartment. Which was about three weeks ago. 

It feels like a lifetime, honestly. Three weeks of just... waking up in a bed that isn't mine, staring at a ceiling fan that makes this weird clicking noise, and just feeling completely empty. It's so strange how quickly it flipped. One minute I was convinced I could optimize the entire global supply chain single-handedly, and the next, I'm sitting on a rented sofa from a corporate housing catalog, unable to even decide what to eat for dinner. It's been exactly three weeks of this heavy, suffocating fog, and it hasn't lifted for a single second. I keep looking at the calendar on my phone, trying to pinpoint exactly when the switch flipped, but it all just blurs together into this one long, exhausting slump since I packed that overnight bag and left the house. Three weeks. It feels like three years.

inference.note: The elevated episode lasted about 7–10 days with marked impairment at work and no psychotic features or hospitalization, meeting criteria for a manic episode. The subsequent 3-week depressive period fits bipolar disorder, current episode manic without psychotic symptoms as the best ICD-10 candidate; unspecified bipolar disorder is no longer needed.

This is followed by a depressive period, but the presence of a manic episode establishes bipolar affective disorder; current/most clearly evidenced index elevated episode is consistent with mania without psychotic symptoms.
